newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea opposition leader calls for OECD delay.
newsitem.headline: South Korea opposition leader calls for OECD delay.

text.p: South Korea's main opposition leader, warning the country was in economic crisis, called on Monday for a delay in joining the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) rich-nation's club.
Kim Dae-jung also demanded deep cuts in government spending to reduce inflationary pressure.
"The government's plan to join the OECD should be delayed by two to three years given the economic weakness," Kim told a news conference.

South Korea, which has the world's 11th largest economy, is hoping the OECD governing council will approve its membership at a September 26 meeting. But opposition parties have opposed the market-opening measures necessary to gain acceptance to the Paris-based group.
Membership must be approved by South Korea's parliament in which President Kim Young-sam's ruling party has only a wafer-thin majority.
"Our economy is now in total crisis due to the government's inconsistent economic policies," Kim Dae-jung said.
"The government should initiate a frugality drive to overcome the current economic crisis."
He said growth of government budget spending for next year should be lowered to 11 percent from a proposed 14 percent.

Kim Dae-jung, who is expected to run for the presidency, said an 11 percent spending increase was appropriate given forecast economic growth for 1997 of six percent and consumer inflation of five percent.

"The government's lenient budget plan looks aimed at improving the ruling party's standing in the presidential elections next year. It is not justifiable because of the danger of inflation," Kim said.
Elections are scheduled for December, and President Kim Young-sam's single term expires in February.
Kim Dae-jung also proposed that the government eliminate unnecessary ministries and streamline state industries.
"Ministries like Interior, Government Administration, Information and Political Affairs should be abolished," he said.
"State-run companies that must be privatised should be privatised. More private managers should be recruited into the government sector," he said.
The government should freeze fares for public untilities, a main contributor to consumer inflation, by the end of 1997 to keep other prices stable.
But Kim, in a clear reference to moves by Korea's big industrial conglomerates to freeze spending on wages, said workers should not be made to suffer.
"It is not fair to demand workers' sacrifice. We have no right to blame their right to demand their fair share within productivity increase," he said.
He also proposed talks on the economy between President Kim and opposition leaders.
